description: The fonu, the giant sea turtle of Samoan tradition, is a sacred guardian called I'a sa ('sacred fish'), believed to save lost fishermen by carrying them to shore. In the celebrated Turtle and Shark legend of Vaitogi, a neglected brother and sister became turtle and shark, appearing when villagers sing their summoning song. Turtle flesh was reserved for high chiefs, and harming turtles was tapu.

description: Eigigu, 'the moon bride,' is the luminous woman of Nauruan mythology who dwells on the moon, governing its cycles and the tides of the surrounding lagoon. Said to weave baskets of light, she appears radiant in the full moon and is regarded as a benevolent, rhythmic figure in Nauruan cosmology, embodying feminine divinity and the cyclical nature of time.

description: Pa'itele is a monstrous sea creature of Samoan legend that terrorized the Apolima Strait, overturning and attacking the canoes that crossed the channel between Upolu and Savai'i. According to oral tradition, the hero Alo eventually defeated the beast, ending its assaults on voyagers. The tale stands as a Samoan hero narrative about courage and the mastery of dangerous waters.

description: Pangkarlangu are fearsome child-stealing monsters of Warlpiri Jukurrpa (Dreaming) stories from Australia's Western and Central Desert. Huge, hairy beings without necks and with sharp claws, they seize children by the legs and carry them off to eat, and their presence marks dangerous desert places. The tale 'The Pangkarlangu and the Lost Child' teaches children to stay near camp and obey elders.

description: Pekapeka is the Māori name for the bat, New Zealand's only native land mammal, a creature of the night tied to omens in traditional belief. In some accounts the night-flying bird hōkioi, whose cry was said to foretell death, is linked to pekapeka, and bats could act as messengers of the spirit world. Conservation efforts now use pekapeka for the two surviving native bat species.

description: Pele is the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fire, lightning, and dance, who dwells in Halema'uma'u crater at Kīlauea. As both creator and destroyer, she builds new land through eruptions and consumes it again, and she is said to produce 'Pele's hair,' the fine threads of volcanic glass found near her vents. Still actively revered today, she is among the most venerated figures of Hawaiian religion.
research_notes: Pele is thoroughly documented in Hawaiian religion and scholarship. Note: the input archetype 'water-spirit' is inaccurate — Pele is a fire/volcano deity; description reflects the documented reality.

description: Patupaiarehe (also Tūrehu) are fairy-like people of Māori lore, fair-skinned with reddish-blond hair and no tattoos, dwelling in misty forests and mountains. Nocturnal and shy, they avoid sunlight and cooked food and sometimes lured humans away to bear red-haired children. The subtribe Ngāti Rua is said to live on Mt Ngongotahā, sometimes read as Aotearoa's pre-Māori inhabitants.
